concept_name: Rolling Friction — Rolling Resists Motion Far Less Than Sliding
source_book: NCERT Class 11 Physics Ch.5 §5.9 (Laws of Motion — Friction, rolling friction paragraph) — table-of-contents scope only, teaching authored from first principles. The atomic idea: rolling contact resists motion two to three orders of magnitude less than sliding contact, obeying the SAME law f = μN with a far smaller coefficient (μᵣ ≈ 0.002 versus μₖ ≈ 0.40) — same mass, same push, opposite outcome. Does NOT cover rotational dynamics (no torque, no moment of inertia, no angular acceleration — the wheel's rendered spin is a kinematic fact, never a dynamics claim), and does NOT re-teach static vs kinetic friction (sibling friction_force owns that arc; this concept deliberately authors μₛ = μₖ = 0.40 on the block to keep exactly one coefficient per body). DC Pandey §8.7 table of contents consulted for scope only — no teaching method, example, or figure imported. Built on the newtons_laws_body field_3d engine (docs/NEWTONS_LAWS_BODY_ENGINE_SPEC.md), Branch A + SEAM G (bodies[].shape:'wheel') + SEAM I (shared_applied_force), zero renderer edits.

real_world_anchor.primary: A suitcase with wheels versus dragging the same suitcase. Dragging it across the floor takes a large steady pull, and stopping for a moment means starting again is hard. Tip it onto its wheels and one finger keeps it moving. Same suitcase, same weight, same floor — the only change is rolling contact instead of sliding contact. That single change divides the friction by about two hundred, and it is the whole reason heavy objects are moved on wheels.
real_world_anchor.secondary: A loaded trolley or cart: the heavier the load, the more dragging becomes impossible while rolling stays easy.

F.name: applied push — both bodies' authored value in every guided state; the one shared engine slider (shared_applied_force:true drives both bodies together, STATE_5 only)

mu_s_block.name: block's coefficient of static friction (sliding contact) — identity constant, never a live control in this concept

mu_k_block.name: block's coefficient of kinetic friction (sliding contact) — identity constant, never a live control in this concept

mu_s_wheel.name: wheel's coefficient of static friction (rolling contact) — identity constant; the stuck-check it feeds is physically inert here since drive is never near zero while it would matter

mu_k.name: wheel's coefficient of kinetic/rolling friction (μᵣ) — the ONE live μ control in this concept, exposed only in STATE_3

theta.name: incline angle — fixed at 0 throughout; flat concept, block_on_incline owns the incline arc

f_block.formula: friction on the block, N — magnitude equals |drive| while stuck (never exceeds mu_s_block*N_block); mu_k_block*N_block once sliding

f_wheel.formula: friction on the wheel, N — magnitude equals |drive| while stuck (never exceeds mu_s_wheel*N_wheel); mu_k*N_wheel once rolling

friction_ratio.formula: f_block / f_wheel at equal N — 0.40/0.002 = 200, the S1/S2 taught number

constraints: f = mu * N in BOTH regimes — the block (sliding, mu = 0.40) and the wheel (rolling, mu about 0.002) obey the SAME law; only which mu applies differs, never a separate rolling-resistance law

rolling resistance is small but never zero: f_wheel = mu_k_wheel * N_wheel is greater than zero for any N_wheel greater than zero — a coasting wheel under rolling friction alone is always decelerating, never coasting forever

both frictions scale with load: N_block = m*g and N_wheel = m2*g, so doubling either mass doubles that body's maximum friction — but only the sliding side's growth can cross a fixed push and flip motion to no-motion

a body at rest with |drive| <= mu_s*N stays at rest, and its reported friction equals the drive exactly, not mu_s*N — this self-adjusting mechanism belongs to friction_force and is only cited once here, in STATE_4, never re-derived

no rotational dynamics anywhere: no torque, no moment of inertia, no angular acceleration is computed or asserted — the wheel's rendered spin is a position-derived kinematic fact (s = r*theta, SEAM G), never a dynamics claim
theta = 0 throughout: N = m*g exactly for every body in every state, never resolved into components — the incline decomposition belongs to block_on_incline

aha_moment.statement: Rolling friction is about 200 times smaller than sliding friction — same push, opposite outcome.
aha_moment.visual_confirmation: Both bodies push with 20 N; the wheel crosses the 11 m track in 2.35 s while the block has moved only 0.76 m by 12 s — the friction readouts show why: 19.6 N vs 0.10 N.

STATE_1.title: Same Push: Rolling Moves Much Farther

scene_composition.text: Same 20 newton push on both bodies, same mass
the wheel crosses the track in about two seconds; the block barely moves
like a suitcase on wheels versus dragging the same suitcase

tts_sentences.text_en: Same mass, same 20 newton push, different results.
The wheel crosses the whole track in about two seconds; the block barely moves.
Sliding friction opposes 19.6 N of the 20 N push, leaving 0.4 N; the wheel's rolling friction opposes only about 0.10 N.

scene_composition.text: One law covers both bodies: f equals mu times N
mu is 0.40 for the block's sliding contact, 0.002 for the wheel's rolling contact
the wheel's push and friction are too small to draw as arrows here

tts_sentences.text_en: One law covers both: friction f equals the friction coefficient mu times normal force N — 0.40 for the block, 0.002 for the wheel.
Same law, far smaller number: both now glide at the same 1.0 meter per second.
The wheel's push and friction are too small to draw, read the number instead: 0.10 newton.

STATE_3.title: Rolling Friction Is Not Zero
STATE_3.motion_archetype: ramp-track (declared contrast pair with STATE_2's reveal-build)

scene_composition.text: The wheel coasts with no push at all
friction reads about 0.10 newton, not zero, and speed keeps slowly falling
raise the friction coefficient, as soft ground would, and the wheel stops

tts_sentences.text_en: The wheel coasts with no push, yet friction reads about 0.10 newton, not zero, too small to draw — and speed keeps falling.
Zero friction would keep speed constant forever; this does not.
Raise the friction coefficient mu, as soft or deformed ground would, and the wheel stops completely; ball bearings make mu even smaller.

misconception_watch.belief: A wheel has no friction — rolling means frictionless.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: The f readout is 0.10 N while the wheel coasts, and the v readout falls the whole time — zero friction would keep v constant forever.
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: Rolling friction is small, not zero — f = μᵣN with μᵣ about 0.002, and it grows on soft or deformed surfaces.

STATE_4.title: Heavier Load: Sliding Stops, Rolling Continues

scene_composition.text: Load doubles to 10 kilograms on both bodies
block's maximum friction is now 39.2 newtons, more than the 20 newton push — it stays still
wheel's friction is only 0.20 newton — it still rolls, slower only because it is heavier

tts_sentences.text_en: The load doubles to 10 kilograms: the block's maximum static friction is now 39.2 newtons, more than its 20 newton push, so it stays still, while the wheel's rolling friction reaches 0.20 newton, too small to draw.
It moves slower than before only because it is heavier now, not because rolling friction grew large.

scene_composition.text: drag mass, push, and starting speed — watch the block and the wheel respond

tts_sentences.text_en: Now change the mass, the push, and the starting speed yourself, and watch the block and the wheel respond.

regeneration_variants.label: A Loaded Delivery Cart: Rolling vs Dragging the Same Load
regeneration_variants.physical_world: A loaded delivery cart resists a steady drag across the floor, but tip it onto its wheels and the same load moves with a light, steady push.
regeneration_variants.same_physics: Identical two-hundred-times friction gap: rolling contact obeys the same f = μN law as sliding contact, just with a coefficient about two hundred times smaller — only the labeled world changes.
regeneration_variants.scene_hint: Same two-body rig, same flat floor — only the labeled objects change from a generic block and wheel to a dragged cart and a wheeled cart.

regeneration_variants.label: An Office Chair: Rolling on Casters vs Sliding It Directly
regeneration_variants.physical_world: Sliding an office chair across a floor by its seat takes real effort; the same chair on its caster wheels glides away from a light push.
regeneration_variants.same_physics: Same contrast, same law: caster wheels give a rolling contact whose friction coefficient is about two hundred times smaller than the chair's sliding contact with the floor.
regeneration_variants.scene_hint: Same rig, same push — only the labeled objects change from a generic block and wheel to a slid chair and a wheeled chair.
